source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: The paper criticises expected utility as a description of risky choice and proposes prospect theory. Method: short questionnaires of hypothetical gambles, anonymous, at most a dozen problems per booklet, several orders, left-right positions swapped.
numbers: Respondents were Israeli students and faculty; amounts in Israeli pounds (median family monthly income about 3,000). Some problems repeated with students and faculty in Stockholm and Michigan with 'essentially identical' results.
limits: Hypothetical, not paid. Authors say they are 'keenly aware' of this and argue real-money tests share other flaws. Small groups (N 64-141 per problem).
agent_relevance: Background for us. Shows the effects come from simple choice prompts, which is how LLM tests are run too.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Certainty effect, Allais type. Problem 1: 2,500 at .33 (2,400 at .66, 0 at .01) vs sure 2,400. Problem 2: 2,500 at .33 vs 2,400 at .34. Most take the sure thing in P1 and the bigger gamble in P2, which breaks expected utility.
numbers: P1 N=72: 82% choose sure 2,400. P2 N=72: 83% choose 2,500 at .33. 61% made the modal choice in both. P3 N=95: 80% sure 3,000 over (4,000,.80). P4 N=95: 65% pick (4,000,.20) over (3,000,.25). Non-money tour, P5 N=72: 78% sure England tour; P6 N=72: 67% pick 5% three-country tour over 10% England.
limits: Hypothetical choices, one sample per problem.
agent_relevance: The same pair of questions is a cheap bias probe for an agent: ask both versions and check consistency.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Ratio violation of substitution at very low probabilities. People prefer the higher-probability prospect when chances are large, but the larger prize when both chances are tiny.
limits: Hypothetical choices.
agent_relevance: Probability-ratio sensitivity depends on where on the 0-1 scale you are. Relevant when an agent compares options with small chances.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Reflection effect. Reverse the sign of outcomes and the majority preference reverses: risk averse for gains, risk seeking for losses.
limits: Earlier sign-flip evidence: Markowitz 1952, Williams 1966 (as cited in the paper). Hypothetical choices.
agent_relevance: Same facts framed as gains or losses draw opposite risk attitudes. An agent's answer should not depend on that unless the reference point is real.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Isolation effect. Same final odds, different presentation, different choice. A two-stage game (75% end, 25% reach stage two and then choose (4,000,.80) or 3,000, choice made before play) equals P4 in final-state terms but people answer it like P3.
numbers: Problem 10: 141 subjects, 78% chose the sure 3,000 branch, against 35% for (3,000,.25) in P4 (N=95). Probabilistic insurance, P9 N=95: 80% would not buy.
limits: Hypothetical choices. Authors say people cancel components shared by both options.
agent_relevance: Choices follow how the problem is sliced, not final outcomes. Restating in final-state form (our schema's restate step) would block this.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Gains and losses are coded relative to a reference point, not final wealth. Two groups got different starting bonuses, faced identical final-state choices, and preferences flipped.
numbers: P11 N=70: given 1,000 first, 84% chose sure 500 over (1,000,.50). P12 N=68: given 2,000 first, 69% chose (-1,000,.50) over sure -500. In final states both equal (2,000,.50;1,000,.50) vs 1,500.
limits: Between-subject, hypothetical. The paper says the reference point can also move with formulation and expectations.
agent_relevance: Reference-point control. In an agent prompt, what counts as the current state changes the answer. State it explicitly.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: The formal model. Two phases: editing (coding, combination, segregation, cancellation, simplification, dominance detection) then evaluation. For regular prospects V(x,p;y,q)=pi(p)v(x)+pi(q)v(y); pi is a decision weight, not a probability.
numbers: v(0)=0, pi(0)=0, pi(1)=1. Strictly positive or negative prospects: V = v(y)+pi(p)[v(x)-v(y)] (riskless part not weighted). Properties: subcertainty pi(p)+pi(1-p)<1; subproportionality; small p overweighted (pi(p)>p); subadditive for small p.
limits: Works for simple prospects with at most two nonzero outcomes. Can violate stochastic dominance, so the 1992 cumulative version was built. Order of editing operations is under-specified, the authors admit.
agent_relevance: Editing phase resembles our restate and decompose steps. The model describes intuitive choice, not advice for the agent.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk
finding: Value function: defined on gains and losses from a reference point, concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper for losses. Loss aversion inferred from dislike of symmetric 50-50 bets. Low-probability overweighting shown by lottery and insurance choices.
numbers: Argument: v(x) < -v(-x) and v'(x) < v'(-x). Bets (x,.50;-x,.50) get less attractive as x grows. P14 N=72: 72% take (5,000,.001) over sure 5; P14' N=72: 83% prefer sure loss 5 over (-5,000,.001). No numeric lambda in 1979.
limits: 1979 gives shape only, no fitted parameters. The 2.25 appears in 1992.
agent_relevance: Origin of 'losses loom larger'. The 1979 argument rests on symmetric bets, the design later critics question.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1992) Advances in prospect theory: cumulative representation of uncertainty
finding: Cumulative prospect theory (CPT) uses rank-dependent cumulative weights, separate weighting functions for gains and losses, and applies to uncertain as well as risky prospects with any number of outcomes. Two principles: diminishing sensitivity and loss aversion. Confirms a fourfold pattern of risk attitudes.
numbers: Fourfold pattern: risk averse for gains of high probability, risk seeking for gains of low probability, risk seeking for losses of high probability, risk averse for losses of low probability.
limits: Only the publisher abstract page was read (full text paywalled). Parameter numbers below come from citing papers.
agent_relevance: CPT is the model most LLM studies fit; its parameters are the yardstick.

source: Citations of Tversky & Kahneman (1992) in Ethayarajh et al. (KTO), Brown et al. (2024), Tarabeih (2026)
finding: Second-hand but consistent: the 1992 medians are alpha=beta=0.88 and lambda=2.25. Weighting is w(p)=p^g/(p^g+(1-p)^g)^(1/g). Tarabeih quotes gamma 0.65.
numbers: Brown et al.: original sample was 25 graduate students from elite west-coast US universities, three unincentivised sessions; only the median 2.25 was reported, no mean or spread. KTO: median alpha 0.88, lambda 2.25.
limits: The 1992 original was not read in full. Separate gains/losses weighting values (about 0.61 and 0.69) are NOT verified in any opened text.
agent_relevance: The 2.25 default comes from 25 students, yet it is the default in finance simulations and in AI loss functions (KTO). Do not hard-code it.

source: Brown, Imai, Vieider & Camerer (2024) Meta-analysis of empirical estimates of loss aversion (J. Economic Literature)
finding: Largest meta-analysis: 607 estimates from 150 articles (1992-2017). Mean lambda 1.955 (95% CrI 1.820 to 2.105), below the original 2.25. Few study features explain the variation.
numbers: Raw: mean 1.97, median 1.69, 93.9% of estimates above 1. Model M1 mean 1.809 [1.740,1.878]; robust M2 1.955 [1.820,2.105]. Aggregate-level mean 1.95; individual-level means 2.94 (skewed). Meta-regression benchmark study 1.984 [1.593,2.385].
limits: Mixes designs and definitions; the Koszegi-Rabin definition gives higher values (2.25 in T&K is 3.35 in KR, per DellaVigna). Yechiam & Zeif re-analyse the same data and get lower values for symmetric designs.
agent_relevance: Typical loss weight is about 2, not 2.25, and varies. A scaffold should not assume a fixed loss weight.

source: Brown et al. (2024)
finding: Publication bias and moderators. Higher lambda estimates are less precise and small lambda seem missing. Bias-corrected mean 1.742 [1.674,1.811]. Field experiments and general-population samples give higher lambda than lab students; surveys give lower than binary lottery tasks; no money vs non-money difference; functional form and reference-point type matter little.
numbers: Publication-bias parameter 1.434 [1.008,1.876]. Guess test at ESA 2019: 37 guesses, mean 1.639, SD 0.599; 20 of 34 low confidence; 24.3% fell between 1.8 and 2.1.
limits: Authors warn funnel asymmetry may reflect heterogeneity as well as bias. Right-skewed distribution.
agent_relevance: Experts themselves guess below 2.25. The 2.25 figure works as an anchor.

source: Brown et al. (2024), review of earlier meta-analyses
finding: Earlier meta-analyses: Neumann & Bockenholt (2014) on 109 estimates from 33 consumer brand-choice studies, lambda 1.49 (base) and 1.73 (enhanced). Walasek, Mullett & Stewart re-fit one CPT model to raw data of 19 estimates from 17 articles, lambda 1.31. Mrkva et al. used five field surveys with 17,720 subjects.
numbers: 1.49 and 1.73 (brand choice); 1.31 (mixed lotteries re-estimated); 17,720 respondents (Mrkva).
limits: Read as reported inside Brown et al., not in the original papers.
agent_relevance: Different inclusion rules move the answer from 1.3 to 2.0. The topic is contested.

source: Ruggeri et al. (2020) Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Large preregistered multinational replication of the 1979 methods. 94% of items replicated with some attenuation; 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated; 100% replication in some countries. Conclusion: the empirical foundations replicate 'beyond any reasonable thresholds'.
numbers: n = 4,098 participants, 19 countries, 13 languages; every participant answered every item; only currencies adjusted. Between-country and within-person heterogeneity reported.
limits: Abstract page only (paywalled). It tests the 1979 choice patterns, not the lambda size. Tarabeih cites its human ranges: curvature 0.41-0.96, weighting 0.53-0.79.
agent_relevance: The qualitative patterns (certainty effect, reflection, fourfold) are real. Loss aversion size is the weaker part.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect theory in large language models: a meta-analysis (arXiv 2610.33103)
finding: First meta-analysis of PT parameters fitted to LLM risky choice: 102 estimates, 11 studies, 32 models. Pooled lambda 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46), far below Brown et al. 1.96 but near the conservative human values 1.31 and 1.07.
numbers: 28 loss-aversion estimates; range 0.49 (Llama3-8B) to 2.72 (GPT-3.5). Against 1: t(27)=2.66, p=.013. 95% prediction interval 0.20 to 2.31. Model-level pooling (19 models) 1.26 [1.02,1.49]. Study level (10 studies) 1.31 [1.06,1.56].
limits: Standard errors partly imputed; repeated runs of one model are not independent people; only 10 studies for lambda. Adding back estimates at fitting bounds: 1.42 [1.00,1.84]. Egger p=.58, low power.
agent_relevance: Most LLMs are not strongly loss averse in plain described gambles. Do not assume a human-like loss bias, and do not assume none.

source: Tarabeih (2026)
finding: Design matters in LLMs as in people. With symmetric gains and losses LLMs show lambda 1.15 (human 1.07 for such designs); with smaller losses than gains LLMs show 1.46 against about 2.3 for humans.
numbers: L=G: 18 estimates, 7 studies, 1.15 [0.98,1.32] (vs 1.07 p=.44; vs Brown 1.96 p<.001). L<G: 10 estimates, 4 studies, 1.46 [0.96,1.96] vs 2.3 (t=-3.81, p=.004). Certainty-equivalent tasks 1.10 [0.79,1.40]; direct choice 1.20 [0.96,1.43].
limits: The human 2.3 vs 1.07 split comes from one source (Yechiam & Zeif 2025).
agent_relevance: Suggests human loss aversion is partly a design contrast effect, which LLMs do not show.

source: Tarabeih (2026)
finding: Moderators of LLM loss aversion: model family explains 27% of variance; Gemini +0.69 above GPT (p=.021), small open models about -0.49 (p=.063), Claude and Qwen not different from GPT. Newer release lowers lambda by 0.16 per year; larger stakes raise it by 0.35 per tenfold increase (p=.030).
numbers: Model 5 coefficients: Gemini 0.86 (SE 0.24), release year -0.25 (0.07), log10 stake 0.31 (0.15), persona 0.49 (0.42, ns). Intercept 1.08. k=28.
limits: Exploratory; year effect rests largely on the GPT lineage in one study; cluster-robust tests have few degrees of freedom.
agent_relevance: Behaviour differs by model, so any scaffold test must be repeated per model.

source: Tarabeih (2026)
finding: Curvature and probability weighting in LLMs. Under the Tversky-Kahneman fit value curvature is near linear (pooled about 1.01, human 0.67); under the Tanaka fit it is more concave than people (0.52 vs 0.67). Probability weighting is inverse-S: 0.81 (TK) and 0.84 (Tanaka).
numbers: Gain curvature 1.04 [0.98,1.11], loss curvature 1.06 [0.92,1.21]; prediction interval 0.69 to 1.33. Weighting 0.81 vs 1 (t(22)=-2.35, p=.028), compatible with human 0.68 (p=.12) and T&K 0.65 (p=.055); without outlier GPT-4.1 (2.17) 0.77 [0.64,0.91]; without Ge et al. 0.65 [0.33,0.96]. GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-30B-Thinking all 0.81.
limits: Only 4 weighting studies; study-level interval [0.37,1.25] includes 1. Fitting method and sample are confounded. A GPT-5.1 row in Ge et al. looks misreported (author note).
agent_relevance: Reasoning models do not remove probability distortion. Probability weighting is the most human-like piece.

source: Tarabeih (2026), supplement S1 citing Yechiam & Tarabeih (2026)
finding: LLM loss aversion depends on the literature it is given: shown a paper reporting strong loss aversion, ChatGPT and Qwen became loss averse; shown one reporting weak or absent loss aversion, lambda stayed between 1.0 and 1.1 (baselines 1.05 and 1.09).
numbers: Baselines 1.05 and 1.09; weak-literature condition 1.0-1.1.
limits: Secondary report of a study the author coauthored.
agent_relevance: The measured bias is partly a response drawn out by the prompt, not a fixed preference.

source: Jia, Yuan, Pan, McNamara & Chen (2024) Decision-making behavior evaluation framework for LLMs under uncertain context
finding: Multiple-price-list fit of risk preference, probability weighting and loss aversion for three commercial LLMs, 300 queries each. All three are risk averse. ChatGPT-4-Turbo has the lowest loss concern and a weighting parameter above 1; Claude-3-Opus has higher loss aversion and overweights small probabilities.
numbers: From the appendix table (layout garbled, check against paper): ChatGPT-4-Turbo risk 0.6031, weighting 1.1819, loss aversion 1.4786 (SD 0.345); Claude-3-Opus weighting 0.7613, loss aversion 6.316 (SD 2.84). 300 draws per model.
limits: Claude lambda 6.3 is flagged as a boundary-type fit by Tarabeih and dropped. Gemini row unclear. Persona prompts shifted parameters further.
agent_relevance: Vendors differ a lot. One model's profile does not carry over.

source: Ross, Kim & Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the behavioral biases of LLMs via utility theory
finding: Fitted CPT value and weighting functions from certainty equivalents for GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo, the only models that passed a monotonic-switching competence test. No probability distortion for gains (more rational than people); GPT-4 Turbo distorts loss probabilities more than people; risk seeking toward losses like humans.
numbers: 56 game settings, 100 samples per setting at temperature 1.
limits: Values shown in figures only. GPT-4 Turbo is less reliable on losses.
agent_relevance: Many models cannot hold a consistent switching point, so raw prompting is an unstable measuring tool.

source: Ross, Kim & Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the behavioral biases of LLMs via utility theory
finding: Prompting changes behaviour little. Direct 'be loss averse' prompts and zero-shot chain of thought barely moved GPT-4; one-shot examples worked; two-shot examples confused gains and losses.
numbers: 56 settings, N=10 per setting. Direct prompt made the loss-side value function more concave, the opposite of expected.
limits: Small N; one model.
agent_relevance: Telling an agent to be careful about losses is weak; worked examples are stronger.

source: Ethayarajh, Xu, Muennighoff, Jurafsky & Kiela (2024) KTO: model alignment as prospect theoretic optimization
finding: Uses the CPT value function as a training loss: 'human-aware losses' (HALOs). DPO and PPO-Clip are shown to be HALOs. KTO maximises utility of generations from a binary desirable/undesirable signal and matches or exceeds DPO from 1B to 30B.
numbers: lambda_D and lambda_U replace the single lambda, default 1 each. Up to 90% of desirable examples can be dropped (1:10 ratio, set lambda_U=1, lambda_D in 10-15) and KTO still beats DPO. Canonical alpha 0.88 and lambda 2.25 quoted.
limits: Uses a CPT-shaped function, does not claim the model is loss averse. Too high lambda hurts BBH and GSM8K.
agent_relevance: Prospect theory as an engineering tool, not a behaviour. Background only for a no-training scaffold.

source: Wang, Liu, Wang & Liu (2026) Developmental trajectories of decision making and affective dynamics in LLMs
finding: Approach-avoidance PT model fitted to successive OpenAI models in a gambling task. Loss aversion falls with each version: 2.72 (GPT-3.5) to 0.57 (GPT-4.1), below neutral. GPT-4 and GPT-4o are comparable to humans. Choices also became more deterministic.
numbers: ANOVA on lambda across versions F=35.87, p<.001, partial eta2=0.481; GPT-4.1<GPT-4o/GPT-4<GPT-3.5 (ts>2.262, ps<.027, d>0.584); humans comparable to GPT-4/4o (ps>.843), different from GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.1 (ps<.001). Risk aversion: no version effect (F=2.37, p=.074).
limits: One lineage, one task; the System-2 explanation is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Newer aligned models lose the human loss bias and move toward expected value.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 shows framing and endowment effects, plus anchoring and representativeness, like people. Framing: efficacy rating 5 in the positive frame vs 4 in the negative frame in all 11 trials; humans 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
numbers: ChatGPT 11 of 11 trials identical (5 vs 4); humans mean 5.2 (CI 5.03-5.37) vs 4.6 (4.35-4.85).
limits: Not a CPT fit; ChatGPT ratings had zero variance. Authors say effect may come from language patterns rather than loss aversion.
agent_relevance: Gain or loss wording alone shifts an LLM's judgement. Framing is a testable weakness.

source: Yechiam & Tarabeih (2026) Mimicry without understanding: the origins of decision bias in LLMs
finding: LLMs show loss aversion when it is described as a bias, and the strength of the bias in a scientific report predicts the models' own later bias. 'Scientific papers of biases can thus become self-fulfilling prophecies' for LLMs.
numbers: ChatGPT-4o lambda 1.257 and 1.218 (loss-aversion condition, large and small sample) vs 1.072 (gain-seeking). Qwen 1.742 vs 0.940 and 0.929.
limits: Four studies, two models; simple lambda formula (accepted loss relative to win).
agent_relevance: Prompts that describe a bias can induce it. Be careful what descriptions and examples the scaffold puts in context.

source: Corazzini, Deriu & Guerzoni (2025) Decision and gender biases in LLMs: a behavioral-economic perspective
finding: Qwen-2.5-32B in a gambling game, neutral and gender personas: near risk-neutral for gains (alpha 1.062), nearly linear weighting for gains (1.001), moderate loss side (beta 0.932, loss weighting 0.800) and loss aversion 1.542, below the human 2.25.
numbers: Loss aversion 1.542; human reference alpha 0.88, lambda 2.25. Models were Gemma-7B and Qwen-2.5-32B; the numbers quoted are for the model the text describes.
limits: Two models, one task; gender effects described as subtle. The text I read does not name which model the quoted row is for.
agent_relevance: LLMs show an attenuated, hybrid profile.

source: Marks & Vollberg (2026) The psychophysics of affect in large language models
finding: Ten LLMs rated how gains and losses would feel. Rated alone: diminishing sensitivity like humans, but gains rated more intensely than equal losses ('silicon gain amplification'). Rated together: ratings linearised and the gain-loss gap mostly vanished; in choice little loss aversion remained.
numbers: Ten models (nine post-trained, one base). Rating scale larger for gains than losses in eight of nine post-trained models.
limits: Rating task and choice; abstract-level numbers only read.
agent_relevance: The same model shows or hides the bias depending on how the question is posed.

source: Du (2025) Mitigating gambling-like risk-taking behaviors in LLMs
finding: Proposes a framework (RARG) with loss-aversion training to cut gambling-like behaviour. Claims 18.7% less overconfidence bias and 24.3% less loss chasing.
numbers: Also claims 52.4% fewer loss-chasing errors on one detector, 21.7% better risk estimation, 12.5% better probability calibration.
limits: Single author; I could not verify the setup behind these numbers. Treat as low reliability.
agent_relevance: Do not use these numbers.

source: Wikipedia 'Prospect theory' (read via WebFetch)
finding: Criticisms listed: reference point hard to define (Koszegi & Rabin 2007); original version violated first-order stochastic dominance; priority heuristic predicts majority choices over 260 problems in four data sets better than CPT; List finds framing effects shrink with market experience; Kachelmeier & Shehata found less support in China with large stakes; a 2017 53-country survey found PT describes lotteries well.
numbers: 260 problems, 4 data sets; 53 countries.
limits: Tertiary source; underlying papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Pointers to competing models for later angles.

source: Wikipedia 'Loss aversion' (read via WebFetch)
finding: Pointers: Gal (2006) and Gal & Rucker (2018) say loss aversion is more simply explained by psychological inertia; Yechiam & Hochman (2013) propose loss attention instead; Yechiam & Zeif (2025) re-meta-analysis says loss aversion is not robust; Mrkva et al. (2020) replicate in five samples; Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler (1990) mug study.
numbers: Mug experiment: 86% of owners kept mugs, 10% of chocolate owners chose mugs, 56% of neither group chose mugs.
limits: Tertiary; Gal & Rucker and Yechiam & Zeif full texts were behind paywalls this session.
agent_relevance: Critics' direction: loss effects may be attention or inertia, which changes how an agent should weigh losses.

source: Yechiam & Zeif (2025) Loss aversion is not robust: a re-meta-analysis (J. Economic Psychology 107, 102801), as reported by Tarabeih (2026)
finding: Re-analysis of the Brown et al. data: human lambda about 1.07 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.18) for symmetric, unordered gain-loss designs; about 2.3 for ordered designs with losses smaller than gains.
numbers: 1.07 [0.97,1.18]; about 2.3 in L<G designs.
limits: Not opened; the paper page redirected and did not load. Numbers via Tarabeih.
agent_relevance: Main challenge to 2.25: it may be largely a design contrast effect.

source: Imai et al. (2025) human meta-analysis of PT curvature and weighting, as used by Tarabeih (2026)
finding: Human benchmark for CPT curvature and weighting: curvature about 0.67 (CI 0.66 to 0.70) and probability weighting about 0.68. Tanaka, Camerer & Nguyen (2010): 0.67 and 0.685.
numbers: Curvature 0.67 [0.66,0.70]; weighting 0.68.
limits: Not opened. Cited in Tarabeih only.
agent_relevance: Reference values to compare an agent against.
